title: One Sentence

scenes.vo: This is a school paddle. In seventeen states, it is still legal.

The school year was twenty twenty-three to twenty twenty-four. American public schools reported corporal punishment of nineteen thousand, eight hundred and fifty-one students. That is not a count of incidents. It is a count of children. Not in nineteen seventy-four. Last year.
highlight: nineteen thousand, eight hundred and fifty-one

scenes.vo: Nineteen thousand, eight hundred and fifty-one students. Twenty-eight thousand, three hundred and ten separate instances, so many of them were struck more than once. In eight hundred and thirty-two districts.

The federal government defines it plainly. Quote: paddling, spanking, or other forms of physical punishment imposed on a child. In the seventeen states that allow it, the law does not require it. It does not recommend it. It permits it, if a local school board says so. And the same board can say no.

fig.eyebrow: U.S. Department of Education · Civil Rights Data Collection
fig.quote: paddling, spanking, or other forms of physical punishment imposed on a child.
fig.sub: In every one of the seventeen states, the decision sits with the local board.

scenes.vo: Take two girls. Same town, same grade, same kind of family, same desk by the window. Call them Ava and Emma. On a Tuesday in October, each of them does the same thing. She shoves a classmate who took her seat. Two schools. Two policies.

Ava's school permits corporal punishment. She is sent to the office, told to bend over a chair, and struck with a wooden board. It is over in a minute. Emma's school prohibits it. She is sent to the office too. Her teacher calls home. She loses recess for a week, and she practices, with an adult, what to do the next time someone takes her seat. It takes a month.

Here is what the research says happens next. Across twenty-one studies in sixty-seven thousand children, girls like Ava are more likely to hit someone again, more likely to be anxious or depressed, and more likely to fall behind in school. Followed into their twenties, they had lower grades, more symptoms of depression, and were more likely to say they would hit their own children one day. And the one thing the paddle was for? Across seventy-five studies, it did not even reliably stop the behavior in the moment. Emma's school used the approach the research does support. Taught expectations. A consequence that fits. Practice. Across fifty-four controlled studies, that is what improved behavior in grades.

left: More likely to hit her own children

scenes.sources: Visser et al. 2022 (21 studies, 67,400 children); Gershoff, Sattler and Holden 2019; Gershoff and Grogan-Kaylor 2016 (75 studies); Korpershoek et al. 2016 (54 studies)
scenes.note: Voice reused from the Texas edition (v3/tts/s07_outcomes.mp3), whose recording reads this wording, not the longer text in script-v3.json; the cards and cues here follow the recording.

scenes.vo: And here is the thing. It is already leaving. In twenty seventeen, American districts reported sixty-nine thousand, four hundred and ninety-two students paddled. Four years later, twenty-four thousand, five hundred and thirty-four. Last year, nineteen thousand, eight hundred and fifty-one. Down seventy-one percent in six years, mostly with no change in the law. Principals and boards are quietly stopping on their own.

fig.eyebrow: U.S. students paddled, as reported by districts
fig.note: in six years.|Mostly with no change in the law.

scenes.vo: Who is it landing on? Of every one hundred students paddled in America, eighty-one are boys. Seventeen have a disability. And the United States Secretary of Education told every governor that Black students are more than twice as likely to be paddled as white students, and Black girls four times as likely as white girls.

fig.eyebrow: Who it lands on · United States, 2023-24

scenes.vo: For the adult holding it, the law offers protection, right up to three words. Excessive. Reasonable. Necessary. Every state that permits it shields staff only for force that follows the board's policy, and that a court later agrees was reasonable. Where the policy is not followed, the protection is gone. Those words are decided afterward, by someone else, who will be shown the research.

rows: No state's protection reaches excessive force: "reasonable but not excessive force" is the common-law rule in every state
Protection runs only to force a court later agrees was reasonable, and only where the board's own policy was followed
Only the force an adult "reasonably believes to be necessary." Restatement (Second) of Torts §147(2); Ingraham v. Wright, 1977

scenes.vo: More than eleven hundred school boards in those seventeen states already prohibit corporal punishment in board policy. In Texas alone, two hundred and ninety-one of them use exactly the same sentence.

scenes.vo: The Board prohibits the use of corporal punishment in the District. That is the whole policy. One sentence, in a policy code every board already has.

fig.eyebrow: The sentence 291 Texas boards adopted, word for word

scenes.vo: More than eight hundred districts still permit it on paper, and did not use it once last year. For those boards, nothing changes on Monday morning except the risk. One sentence. One meeting. And every Ava gets Emma's Tuesday.
